description_full: Dillard's, Inc. operates retail department stores in the southeastern, southwestern, and midwestern areas of the United States. The company offers fashion apparel for men, women, and children; accessories, cosmetics, home furnishings, and other consumer goods through dillards.com, an Internet store and clearance centers. It also engages in the general contracting construction activities, such as constructing and remodeling stores for the company. The company was founded in 1938 and is based in Little Rock, Arkansas.

financial_summary: Dillard's, Inc. is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $9.4B market cap on $6.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -2% over the past three years and -0% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 80% against a 11% cost of capital — a 70-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 35%.

The business throws off $624M in free cash flow — roughly 10 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.26× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 17× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 6.3% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 32% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 14% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 19% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 42% and a beta of 1.18, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.46 vs 5y 1.30), so read it loosely.

val: The stock trades only 10% below its DCF fair value of $673, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 38%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $554 to $832 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 13.8 vs 19.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 261% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 6.6% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.8% (vs the 8% bar).

prof: ROIC of 80% clears the cost of capital of 10.6% by 70pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.14).

ROE of 32% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.0x equity multiplier).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $404.6M.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 8.8, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at -2.1% over 3 years, 8.2% over 5 years and -0.3% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 15%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 26.5% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a backlog worth 2% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 6%.
Capex runs only 0.5x depreciation (1.4% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 31.6% on average.
own: Insiders own 31.6%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 72%.
It returns 6.3% a year to shareholders (1.1% in buybacks and 0.2% in dividends).

Short interest is elevated at 28.6% of the float, 4.8 days to cover.
